claim: Asking why and why-not questions about program output, answered by dynamic slicing, speeds human diagnosis in small lab studies (Whyline: 7.8x on six scenarios, 40% more tasks, N=9; Java: 3x success, 2x speed, N=20; pilot N=9 vs 18 historical controls).
agent_test: Give agent a why/why-not question step then a code-computed backward slice vs free exploration; equal tokens, bug-localisation success.

claim: All Whyline evidence comes from one research group (Ko and Myers), with small samples and tools they built; no independent replication was found. Parnin and Orso 2011 (opened) is an independent study of a different tool (Tarantula ranked list): 24 students, no overall time benefit, benefit only for high performers on the easy task (8:51 vs 14:28, N=10, p<0.05), none on the harder task, and moving the fault in the ranking changed nothing; programmers kept inspecting for 61% of time after seeing the fault.
agent_test: Do not treat human-study speedups as evidence for LLMs; test directly.

claim: Whyline benefit is bounded: hard task 2 succeeded only 4/10 with tool vs 0/10; no speed difference at ceiling; why-didn't questions rarely used when analysis took about a minute; users could not ask about already-happened events in the early prototype.
agent_test: Measure whether agent skips backward step on hard tasks; log question types used.

claim: Most debugging questions are why-didn't (68%) and about a single object (85%); initial human guesses about the cause are wrong about 90% of the time; 50% of Alice errors came from false hypotheses.
agent_test: Count how often agent's first hypothesis is wrong; force a hypothesis-falsification check before editing.

claim: Developers lack support for causal-chain questions: 'what code caused this program state' was unsatisfied 61% of the time (up to 21 min); developers spend about 35% of time on navigation and 42% of dependencies followed were indirect and unsupported.
agent_test: Provide a code-computed dependence navigator tool; compare tool calls and tokens to grep-only agent.
audit: downgraded 2026-11-10 by check_established.py: only 1 opened source(s) from distinct authors

claim: LLMs are poor at producing exact program slices: GPT-4o best static Accuracy-D 60.84% but exact match 7.33%; dynamic exact match 0%; prompt tricks add only about 4 points. Agentic slicing (SliceMate) and execution-estimation (RecovSlicing) improve markedly but on different benchmarks, so not directly comparable.
agent_test: Compute slices with static/dynamic analysis tools, not the model; compare to model-guessed slice on same bugs.

claim: LLM accuracy degrades as the causal chain grows: below 40% when over 20 upstream sources, sharp drop beyond about 600 slice lines or 100 execution steps; runtime-behaviour reasoning averages 44.4% over models. Gap 4: the 20 / 600 / 100 thresholds were read from plots on an abductive value-prediction task (mean slice 393.6 lines, mean chain 93.9 steps); they were never tested as switch points for a tool.
agent_test: Test agent on bugs binned by dependence-chain length; add chunking or tool-computed slice above the threshold.

claim: Giving an LLM a computed slice of the failure improves repair/localisation: CausalRepair removing source slice -26.5% fixes, failing-line-only test -38.3%; BluesFL without instruction path 5 vs 24 Top-1, without signal values cost +609%; SWE-Doctor runtime diagnosis +8.0 points on 50 Pro issues.
agent_test: Ablate the slice context in our agent at equal tokens.

claim: Asking the debugger 'why?' works for LLMs: ChatDBG 57% plain why, 67% targeted question, 85% after one follow-up (10 runs each, gpt-4-1106); only 36% of fixes hit root cause, 55% proximate cause.
agent_test: Plain why vs targeted why vs why plus follow-up on our agent; score root-cause vs proximate fix.

claim: Execution traces and runtime information do not reliably help LLM repair: LDB gives up to +9.8% on small benchmarks, but trace-guided repair beats resampling only on BigCodeBench (26.7 vs 22.4) and loses on LiveCodeBench (4.9 vs 6.5); debug-gym gains vary hugely by model and are absent for some. New: Adnan and Kuhn show traces cost tokens and break even only if calls fall 13-17%; Debug2Fix finds raw debugger tools flat or harmful but a question-answering debug subagent helps (GPT-5 60.2% to 73.1% on GitBug-Java). Pattern: focused answers to a question help, raw trace dumps often do not; model strength and benchmark also matter.
agent_test: Equal-token comparison of trace-augmented repair vs resampling on 3 benchmarks.

claim: Model-generated explanations or feedback can mislead: wrong model explanations hurt SD on StarCoder; self-repair gains vanish when cost is counted; human feedback lifts GPT-4 repair from 33.3% to 52.6%; AutoFL explanations only 20% accurate.
agent_test: Check model's causal explanation against executed evidence before acting on it.

claim: LLM fault localisation is fragile: 78% of previously correct localisations fail after semantic-preserving mutations; faults in the first quarter of code found most often. Gap 9: CausalRepair, which computes slices with a tool, dropped only 7.7% on semantic-preserving rewrites (313 to 289 fixes) vs 15% for ReinFix, so tool-computed slices appear more robust than model-only localisation, on one benchmark.
agent_test: Run agent on mutated copies of the same bug; track consistency.

claim: AutoFL-style tool navigation beats spectrum-based FL (method acc@1 +19.7% Defects4J, +166.7% / +233.3% BugsInPy with GPT-3.5/4); confidence correlates with precision (Spearman 0.52-0.57). Gap 7: confidence tracked Precision@1 at Spearman +0.57/+0.52 but needed five runs per bug; tool-call cap 10 (cap 20 halved performance), mean 5.37 calls. Gating is untested at equal tokens.
agent_test: Use model confidence as a gate for extra backward-search steps.

claim: Weiser's slicing claim is recognition evidence: 21 programmers, 3 programs of 75-150 lines, slices recognised more often than other fragments (second-hand via Parnin and Orso; Ko 2025 earlier line says two programs). Original statistics unverified. Later tests of slicing tools were null or mixed (Weiser and Lyle none; Kusumoto 6 students mixed; Francel and Rugaber 4 of 17 slice instinctively).
agent_test: No direct test; treat as motivation only.

claim: No study found compares a code-computed backward slice with the agent's free exploration at equal tokens on SWE-bench. Indirect evidence: capable agents mostly reach the right functions (60-69% of failures) and fail at edit quality, so localisation has limited headroom for strong models; weak models fail at search (Qwen3-8B 41.1%). SWE-Doctor's runtime diagnosis gains cost more per issue ($0.43 vs $0.23 on Verified).
agent_test: Run the same agent with and without a tool-computed slice at a fixed token budget on bugs split by model strength.

claim: Reproduction tests that do not witness the real fault mislead the agent: SWE-Doctor fail-to-fail tests cost 2-3 issues of 100; VibePass finds non-witnessing self-made tests repair worse than no test, while witnessing ones match external tests. The bottleneck is the fault hypothesis, not test syntax.
agent_test: Before using a self-made reproduction, check it fails for the reported reason (same exception or wrong value).

claim: Asking the model to explain, per candidate, why it could cause the failure improves localisation (RGFL file Hit@1 71.4% to 85%, element exact match 36% to 69%), and a bounded runtime question answered with evidence helps (Debug2Fix +13 to +22% on GitBug-Java). Whether why-not beats why-did or a hypothesis list is untested.
agent_test: A/B: why-not question vs why-did vs hypothesis list at equal tokens.

claim: Bare ranked suspect lists do not give understanding: in Parnin and Orso only 1 of 10 stopped after reaching the fault, others spent 61% of time continuing, and 37% of visits jumped non-linearly.
agent_test: Require the agent to state the causal path from a suspect line to the failing output before accepting it.
